title: Japanese Upper Secondary Informatics: Common Test Washback, Programming Language Diffusion, and Inquiry Erosion
source_name: Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) & National Center for University Entrance Examinations
description: Empirical survey monitoring the diffusion of programming languages (Python vs others), teacher licensure rates, entrance exam preparation drill hours, and autonomous software project development in Japanese high school Informatics I courses.
observation_unit: Secondary school curriculum survey panel across high school tracks in Japan
sample_population_note: Annual survey of public and private upper secondary schools offering compulsory Informatics I (approx. 4,800 schools)
title_ja: 【高校情報科実態調査】共通テスト導入による試験対策特化と探究的プロジェクト開発のトレードオフ

research_angles.title: The Entrance Exam Washback Paradox: How High-Stakes Testing Standardized Python Adoption While Suppressing Creative Software Engineering
research_questions: How has the integration of Informatics into the National Common University Entrance Examination affected classroom instructional allocation?
Does intensive algorithm drill crowd out student autonomous project creation?
hypotheses: Common test preparation hours exhibit a statistically significant negative coefficient on student autonomous project creation.
Teacher specialized licensure acts as a vital buffer against excessive rote test drilling (VIF < 2.0).
research_angles.theoretical_framework: Curricular Washback Theory (Alderson & Wall) and Constructionist Learning Theory (Papert)
